options.text: No federal approval was required
Federal approval was required before the change
Only state approval was needed
options.misconception: confuses state approval with federal preclearance

options.text: Courts review only after enactment

questions.explanation: Preclearance required federal approval before changing voting laws in covered jurisdictions, even for changes claimed to be minor.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The defect in the statutory coverage formula
questions.stem: If a formula's data is 50 years old, how many decades is that?
questions.explanation: 50 years divided by 10 equals 5 decades. The defect was reliance on outdated data to determine coverage.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Language assistance under the voting-rights statute
questions.stem: Leo's log asks what language assistance requires.

options.text: Only English ballots are permitted
options.misconception: confuses official language with voting access

options.text: Language assistance is never required
Ballots and help in the needed language
Voters must bring their own translators

questions.explanation: The statute required language assistance where needed, including ballots and help in the relevant language.
questions.hint: Language assistance is required where needed.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The census and the districts built on it
questions.stem: Maya asks whether a state can skip redistricting after a census.

options.text: Courts redraw districts automatically
Districts are fixed forever once drawn
Only congressional districts need updating
options.misconception: limits census use to federal districts

options.text: Redistricting is needed to reflect population change

questions.explanation: Redistricting reflects population change after the census. Fixed boundaries or automatic court redraws are not the rule.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A question referred to the electorate

stimulus.body: A city council passes an ordinance on zoning and places it on the ballot for voter approval before it takes effect.

questions.stem: Tom asks what the city is using.

options.text: An initiative lets voters propose a new law
A referendum lets voters approve or reject the ordinance
A recall removes an official
A primary selects nominees

questions.explanation: A referendum submits a legislative act to voters for approval or rejection. It is the proper tool here.
questions.hint: Referendum means voter approval of a law.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Initiative and referendum distinguished
questions.stem: Ken asks whether an initiative can be used to remove a governor.

options.text: An initiative approves a law
An initiative removes an official
An initiative proposes a law, not removal of an official
An initiative selects nominees

questions.explanation: An initiative proposes a law by petition. Removing an official requires a recall, not an initiative.
questions.hint: Initiative is for laws, not removals.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A recall and its use
questions.stem: A recall needs 15,000 signatures; 11,500 are collected. How many more?
questions.explanation: 15,000 minus 11,500 equals 3,500 signatures. A recall removes an elected official before term ends.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The purpose of a primary
questions.stem: Priya asks whether a primary winner automatically takes office.

options.text: A primary approves a law
A primary elects the final officeholder
A primary removes an official
A primary only selects the party nominee

questions.explanation: A primary selects the party nominee. The general election, not the primary, elects the officeholder.
